newsitem.title: UK: European buyers resist extra '97 Saudi crude sales.
newsitem.headline: European buyers resist extra '97 Saudi crude sales.

text.p: Supply of crude oil to Europe in 1997 from the world's biggest producer and exporter Saudi Arabia is likely to be little changed from this year despite Riyadh's offer of extra barrels, European oil traders said on Thursday.

Some of Saudi Arabia's 20 term contracts with European customers, worth almost two million barrels a day (bpd), come up for renewal at the turn of the year. Several contract holders told Reuters their Saudi purchases would remain steady.
"From our point of view the negotiations were very easy. We are going to have exactly the same volumes and exactly the same grades," said a middle-ranking term customer.
"The Saudis are offering additional volumes for 1997 but we're quite happy with what we're taking this year," said another.

European oil traders were quick to point out that the offer of extra crude next year did not mean Saudi Arabia was looking to breach its eight million barrels per day (bpd) OPEC quota or engage in a comprehensive reallocation among clients but rather reflected fine-tuning of volumes and grades.
"I don't think there's anything sinister going on. They are making some adjustments but it's all within the tolerance levels," said a European-based U.S. oil company executive.

Traders said Saudi Aramco, which markets about six million bpd of the Kingdom's crude, was offering to restore volumes for some of its smallest customers to levels seen prior to 1995 when production of Arab Heavy was cut back to make room for the new Super Light stream aimed primarily at Asian clients.
"There has been a shuffling of allocations but overall volumes will probably remain unchanged," said a trader.

Industry sources said Aramco may now be looking to shift marginal barrels from Asia to Europe to take advantage of a recent improvement in Atlantic Basin returns and because sales of the new crude have proved disappointing.
Arab Super Light was promoted by Aramco as a way of increasing the country's oil revenue because of the grade's potentially high yields and low sulphur content.
"They pushed prices as high as they could and weren't able to sell much Super Light," said one.

The Brent-Dubai spread, which gives a rough indication of the relative strength of crude markets west and east of the Suez Canal, has widened again this year as depleted stocks of refined products -- particularly heating oil -- in Europe and the U.S. have pushed Brent to new five-year highs.
On the paper market, Brent has been worth an average $1.43 a barrel more than Dubai so far this year, compared to last year's 75 cents.

Others suggest the possibility that 700,000 bpd of Iraqi crude exports will resume some time next year under a stalled U.N. oil-for-food plan may be encouraging the Saudis to try to lock in increased market share.

Earlier this month, Aramco cut prices to European customers for December, taking Arab Light to Dated Brent minus $1.85 a barrel compared with $1.45 this time last year and Arab Medium to Dated Brent minus $3.05, against $2.10 a year ago.

In early July, Saudi Aramco told customers worldwide that fob Ras Tanura liftings of all grades in August would be reduced by five percent because of unusually high nominations and strong domestic summer demand.
The restriction was extended to September for the minority of Aramco's customers who take crude basis fob Sidi Kreir and delivered Rotterdam.
